lines: Routine postnatal checkup with head swelling noted
The infant returns for a routine postnatal checkup following an earlier encounter for murmur evaluation.
He carries a history of congenital rubella syndrome.
The mother reports that the delivery was complicated and required the use of vacuum assistance.
She is concerned about a swelling on the right side of the infant's head that she noticed this morning.
The infant is feeding well and has had no fever or irritability.
- History of ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn

Vital signs are within normal limits.
On examination, the infant is alert and active.
Physical examination reveals a firm, non-tender, well-demarcated swelling that is confined to the right parietal region and does not cross the sagittal suture.
The anterior fontanelle is soft and flat.
The remainder of the examination is unremarkable.

He is brought by his mother due to yellowing of the skin.
The mother is O positive and reports a healthy pregnancy and an uncomplicated vaginal delivery at term.
She mentions that the baby has been breastfeeding well but seems more sleepy than her previous child.

encounters.cc: poor feeding and increased work of breathing

lines: Poor feeding and increased work of breathing
The patient is a male infant with congenital rubella syndrome, recently evaluated for neonatal cephalohematoma and ABO hemolytic disease, who returns for ongoing care.
His mother reports that he breathes rapidly even at rest and takes long pauses while feeding, often falling asleep before finishing his bottle.
She also notes that his pulses feel "strong" and that his breathing seems louder when lying down.
- History of ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn
The baby was born full-term and had normal APGAR scores.
He has not had any cyanosis or fever.
- Ibuprofen lysine 10 mg/kg PO q24h for 3 doses (PDA closure protocol)
- Furosemide 1 mg/kg PO q12h PRN (for symptomatic PDA/CHF management)
- Maternal first-trimester rubella infection (non-immune status during pregnancy)
- Paternal blood type A positive (ABO incompatibility)
- No family history of retinoblastoma or other childhood malignancies (sporadic mutation)
- No family history of congenital heart disease
Physical exam reveals a hyperdynamic precordium and bounding peripheral pulses.
On auscultation, a continuous murmur is heard best at the left infraclavicular area.
There are no signs of hepatomegaly or peripheral cyanosis.
Cardiac catheterization is performed to further evaluate the suspected lesion, and oxygen saturation values are shown in the image.

encounters.cc: noticing a swelling in his right scrotum

lines: Noticing a swelling in his right scrotum
The infant returns for urologic evaluation with a history of congenital rubella syndrome, retinoblastoma, patent ductus arteriosus, and prior neonatal cephalohematoma and ABO hemolytic disease.
The parents report that the swelling seems to be painless, as the infant does not cry or show signs of discomfort when the area is touched.
The infant has been feeding well and has had no fever or vomiting.
His birth history is unremarkable, and he was born at term via spontaneous vaginal delivery without complications.
- History of ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn
- Ibuprofen lysine 10 mg/kg PO q24h for 3 doses (PDA closure protocol)
- Furosemide 1 mg/kg PO q12h PRN (for symptomatic PDA/CHF management)
- Maternal first-trimester rubella infection (non-immune status during pregnancy)
- Paternal blood type A positive (ABO incompatibility)
- No family history of retinoblastoma or other childhood malignancies (sporadic mutation)
- No family history of congenital heart disease
On physical examination, the pediatrician observes a non-tender, smooth, and swollen right hemiscrotum.
Transillumination of the right scrotum reveals a red glow.
The abdomen is soft and non-distended, with no palpable masses.
The rest of the physical examination is within normal limits.

encounters.cc: concerned about a persistent rash on his scalp

lines: Concerned about a persistent rash on his scalp
The patient is a male infant with congenital rubella syndrome, retinoblastoma, and patent ductus arteriosus presenting with a persistent scalp rash.
The rash appeared two weeks ago and has not improved with regular bathing.
The infant is otherwise healthy and meeting all developmental milestones.
- History of ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn
He was born at term without complications.
- Ibuprofen lysine 10 mg/kg PO q24h for 3 doses (PDA closure protocol)
- Furosemide 1 mg/kg PO q12h PRN (for symptomatic PDA/CHF management)
The mother denies any family history of atopic dermatitis or psoriasis.
On examination, the infant is well-appearing and afebrile.
The scalp shows thick, greasy, yellowish scales, and similar lesions are noted on the eyelids and in the nasolabial folds.
There is no evidence of lymphadenopathy, and the rest of the physical examination is normal.

encounters.cc: concerned about a recent change in his behavior and appearance

lines: Concerned about a recent change in his behavior and appearance
This 3-year-old male with congenital rubella syndrome and patent ductus arteriosus returns for assessment of visual changes.
They report that he has been bumping into objects and seems to have difficulty seeing.
His mother also mentions that she noticed a strange glow in his right eye when taking photos of him in dim lighting.
- History of ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn
- Ibuprofen lysine 10 mg/kg PO q24h for 3 doses (PDA closure protocol)
- Furosemide 1 mg/kg PO q12h PRN (for symptomatic PDA/CHF management)
There is no family history of eye diseases
On examination, the pediatrician observes that the child has a white pupillary reflex in the right eye.
The child also has a slight inward deviation of the right eye when trying to focus on an object.
The rest of the physical examination is unremarkable.
